Case Study: The Suez Canal Blockage

March 2021 saw a glaring example of how a single event can ripple through global supply chains. The Suez Canal blockage by the Ever Given container ship halted nearly $9 billion worth of goods a day. This incident delayed shipments of vital goods, including medical supplies, and highlighted the fragility of global trade routes.

Increased Supply Chain Risks Post-COVID

The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated supply chain vulnerabilities. A survey by the Institute for Supply Management found that 75% of companies reported supply chain disruptions in some capacity during the early months of the pandemic. With lockdowns and border closures, the manufacturing sector was hit particularly hard, struggling to maintain regular operations.

Geopolitical Tensions and Their Impact

Geopolitical tensions, such as the trade war between the United States and China, add another layer of complexity. According to Reuters, the U.S. imposed tariffs on $370 billion worth of Chinese goods, which disrupted supply chains for numerous American companies dependent on imports. This has led companies to re-evaluate their supply chain strategies to mitigate these risks.

Natural Disasters: An Ever-Present Threat

Natural disasters also play a major role in disrupting supply chains. The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami in Japan are infamous for causing massive supply chain interruptions, particularly in the automotive and electronics sectors. Toyota and Sony faced significant production halts due to damaged factories and supply shortages.

Data-Driven Case Studies: Insights from Leading Companies

A Gartner report highlighted how companies like FedEx and UPS utilize big data and predictive analytics to minimize risks and navigate disruptions efficiently. Their advanced risk management strategies enable them to offer superior resilience compared to less proactive competitors.

Third-Party Dependencies and Risks

Identifying and managing third-party risks is crucial. For example, companies heavily reliant on just a few suppliers face greater risks. The 2020 Covid-19 pandemic led TSMC, a major semiconductor supplier, to spotlight the vulnerability of tech giants like Apple and Qualcomm to supply chain disruptions.

The Need for Real-Time Supply Chain Visibility

Real-time visibility into supply chain operations is no longer a luxury but a necessity. Integrated digital technologies enable companies to track inventory, monitor real-time risk events, and can swiftly adapt to changing conditions. Companies like Amazon leverage real-time data to predict and manage disruptions effectively.

Supply chains are under more scrutiny than ever. For more strategies on handling value-chain intricacies, consider exploring this strategic approach to privacy and confidentiality.

The spread of certain fake drugs used for malaria or cancer causes serious health, economic, and humanitarian harm [32, 33]. The use of falsified antimicrobial agents has serious public health implications including the rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance with poor infection control [34]. The use of falsified or substandard cardiovascular drugs such as clopidogrel could increase the risk of morbidity and mortality in high-risk patients [35]. Another serious public health problem of SF medical products emerged with the spread of fake coronavirus vaccines in certain parts of the world [36, 37].

The productivity analysis for authors and countries indicated that research on SF medical products occurs in a large number of countries. The leading role of the US and certain European countries was not surprising since (1) it is in those countries where better infrastructures and more abundant resources for research are available [38]; (2) well-established and major pharmaceutical companies exist, and (3) falsified medicines is a global problem and present in developed countries as well as developing ones. India and China ranked 6th and 7th respectively in research productivity in this field. A report released by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) in 2019 claimed that India and China are the leading sources of falsified medicines globally [39]. The report stated that “up to 20 % of drugs sold in the Indian market are falsified and could represent a serious threat to patient health and safety”. However, representatives of the Indian pharmaceutical industry disagree with the US allegation and stated that up to 3.0 % of drugs in India were “not of standard quality”, and 0.02 % were spurious. Drug regulatory agency in India has implemented regulations specifically to fight falsified drugs [30]. China took several steps in the fight against falsified drugs especially after the death of more than a dozen infants in China due to fake milk powder that had little or no nutritional value [40]. China strengthened its regulatory policies after it joined the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in 2001. The WHO calculates that China’s State Drug Administration closed 1,300 illegal factories in 2003 alone [41].

Trofimova E.O., Denisova M.N.
In 2020-2021, COVID-19 pandemic made a significant impact on the pharmaceutical market in developed countries as well as developing ones. Since 2019 the Russian pharmaceutical market has been demonstrating high growth rates in value terms with the main contribution made by the public (reimbursement) sector of the market.The goal was to study the main trends in the medicines consumption in the public sector of the Russian pharmaceutical market.Materials and methods. The analysis was based on IQVIA data, including preferential medicines supply (MS) for outpatients, MS for hospitalized patients, centralized federal MS programs, and other MS. The IQVIA data did not consider the use of COVID-19 vaccines.Results. In 2019-2021, the average annual growth rate of the public sector was 125.4% in value terms, which was determined by shifts in the consumption structure in favor of more expensive drugs. The main contribution to the positive dynamics was made by the hospital segment, share of which increased over the three years by 17 percentage points up to 45%. The dynamics of preferential MS programs lagged the general growth rates. The 1990s were what they call a "lost decade" for the Japanese economy as a whole, and the Port of Kobe was already losing its comparative advantage. However, it was the 1995 Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake that drastically accelerated its decline.

Why do direct and indirect losses matter?

While it is difficult to calculate a global value, evidence at the country level indicates that indirect losses can surpass the direct costs, particularly if economic resilience is low (GFDRR, 2014a; UNISDR, 2015a). Direct losses to the built environment in the Haiti earthquake in 2010 represented 80% of the total direct losses but only 47% of the total (combined direct and indirect) losses (Government of the Republic of Haiti, 2010). However, indirect losses and the wider effects of disaster loss for low-income households and communities are rarely accounted for (UNISDR, 2009b).

This is mostly because it can be difficult to anticipate and quantify the potential for indirect losses despite their size (GFDRR, 2014a). The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami in Japan and flooding in Thailand offer an example of the global indirect impacts from local events (GFDRR, 2014a). Although the Japanese tsunami was much more spectacular and had dramatic news coverage; however, the Thailand floods caused much more damage to industrial supply chains on a global basis (GFDRR, 2014a).

documents.textLong:
. This disrupts communication channels between emergency responders, government agencies, and the affected population.
  • Limited Access to Information: The lack of reliable communication channels hinders access to vital information, such as weather updates, evacuation routes, and the extent of damage. This can impede effective response efforts and lead to confusion and misinformation.
  • Challenges in Coordination: Disrupted communication can lead to coordination challenges between different response agencies, making it difficult to allocate resources efficiently and respond effectively to the needs of the affected population.

  • Satellite Communication: Satellite phones and internet services offer a reliable alternative to terrestrial communication networks, especially in areas where infrastructure has been damaged.
  • Mobile Network Optimization: Network operators can prioritize emergency calls and data traffic, ensuring critical communication channels remain available during disasters.
  • Public Safety Broadband Networks: Dedicated broadband networks for public safety agencies provide high-speed data connections for real-time information sharing and communication.
  • Social Media and Citizen Reporting: Social media platforms can be used to gather information from the public, allowing responders to assess the situation and prioritize resources effectively.

Real-World Examples:

  • During Hurricane Katrina in 2005, satellite phones played a crucial role in communication, as terrestrial networks were severely disrupted.
  • The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami in Japan highlighted the importance of mobile network optimization, as emergency calls surged significantly.
  • The use of social media during the 2010 Haiti earthquake facilitated information sharing and coordination among responders.

The Impact of Telecommunications on Emergency Response Effectiveness

Telecommunications play a crucial role in modern emergency response systems, significantly impacting their effectiveness. By enabling rapid communication, coordination, and resource allocation, telecommunications enhance response times, improve collaboration among responders, and ultimately contribute to better outcomes for those in need.

Improved Response Times

Faster communication is a key factor in reducing response times. Telecommunications technologies, such as mobile phones, two-way radios, and dispatch systems, allow for immediate communication between emergency services and the public. This swift exchange of information enables responders to be dispatched quickly and efficiently, minimizing the time it takes for help to arrive.

Enhanced Coordination and Collaboration

Effective coordination is vital in emergency response. Telecommunications facilitate seamless communication among emergency responders, agencies, and the public. This includes:

  • Real-time updates on incident situations
  • Sharing of critical information among responders
  • Coordination of resources and personnel
  • Collaboration with other agencies, such as law enforcement and healthcare

This enhanced coordination ensures a more efficient and effective response to emergencies

3. Mediterranean-Asian Seismic Belt
  • Description: Extending from the Mediterranean Sea through the Middle East to Asia, this region is marked by active tectonic activity and historical seismic events.
  • Countries Affected: Includes countries like Turkey, Greece, Italy, Iran, and parts of the Middle East.
  • Characteristics: Complex plate interactions, including subduction zones and collision boundaries, create seismic risks and occasional major earthquakes.
4. San Andreas Fault System, United States
  • Description: Located in California, the San Andreas Fault is a prominent transform boundary where the Pacific Plate and the North American Plate meet.
  • Characteristics: Known for producing significant earthquakes, such as the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake.
  • Impact: Regular seismic monitoring and earthquake preparedness measures are critical due to the fault’s proximity to densely populated areas.
5. Japan and Indonesia
  • Description: Both Japan and Indonesia lie in the Pacific Ring of Fire and are characterized by their frequent earthquakes, volcanic activity, and tsunami risks.
  • Impact: The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami in Japan and the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami highlight the devastating effects of seismic events in these regions.
  • Preparedness: Robust earthquake early warning systems and disaster preparedness measures are crucial for minimizing casualties and damage.

Mitigating Seismic Risks

Understanding the world’s most seismically active regions is essential for implementing effective disaster preparedness, building resilient infrastructure, and promoting public awareness. Governments, researchers, and communities in these areas continually work to improve earthquake monitoring, early warning systems, and response strategies to mitigate the impact of seismic events on human lives and infrastructure. By studying the geological processes driving seismic activity and embracing proactive measures, societies can better prepare for and respond to the challenges posed by earthquakes, ensuring safer and more resilient communities in seismic-prone regions globally.

New Zealand Is In Big Trouble, According To Scientists

Robin Andrews

Science & Policy Writer

clockNov 28 2017, 11:48 UTC

Remember, New Zealand is a geologically active country - which is the reason it's so beautiful, from north to south, east to west. jon alkain/Shutterstock

New Zealand made the headlines this time last year after a 7.8M quake rocked both the North and South Islands. For such a powerful tremor, it was lucky only a handful of people were killed – but geoscientists are now warning that the pieces are in place for the next catastrophe.

“One thing about reflecting on from the Kaik?ura earthquake is we don't want people to think this is the big one,” GNS scientist Dr Ursula Cochran told a gathering of scientists in Blenheim earlier this month, per Stuff.co.nz.

New Zealand’s so-called “big one”, a potential 9.0M tremor, is still on its way.

The world’s most powerful earthquakes always occur on these subduction zones. The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami in Japan was a devastating recent example of this, but it appears not much media attention is being given to various subduction zones around the world.

Although the likelihood of a powerful tremor occurring along the San Andreas Fault in the next 30 years is essentially a dead certainty, it’s actually the Pacific Northwest you should watch out for, where the subduction of one plate under the North American plate is building up a lot of stress.

The Hikurangi subduction zone off the eastern seaboard of New Zealand’s North Island is in a similar situation. Here, the oceanic Hikurangi Plateau is sinking beneath the continental crust of the Indo-Australian plate.

The line to the left of the Hikurangi Plateau is the subduction zone in question. Alexrk/Wikimedia Commons; CC BY-SA 3.0

The friction between these colossal pieces of crust builds up stress, and occasionally it’s released during earthquakes of varying intensity. The 7.8M Kaik?ura earthquake in November 2016 took place along the southernmost part of the Hikurangi subduction zone.
